chunks.title: Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Do not pull out an embedded knife, glass shard, or stake. The object may be sealing a severed vessel, and removing it can cause sudden fatal bleeding. Build up padding on either side of the object until the padding is higher than the object, then bandage across the padding without pressing on the object itself. Apply pressure around the object, not on it.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain first aid guidance (WHO/ICRC field manuals)

chunks.title: Bleeding and Wounds
chunks.text: Control the bleeding at the stump first. The casualty's life takes priority over the severed part. Wrap the severed part in clean, slightly damp gauze, seal it in a plastic bag, and place that bag in a second bag containing cold water and ice. Never place the severed part directly on ice or in water. Direct contact with ice causes freezing damage that makes reattachment impossible. Label the bag with the time of injury and keep it with the casualty.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain first aid guidance (WHO/ICRC field manuals)

chunks.title: Breathing and Cardiac Emergencies
chunks.text: If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing. Do not intervene while an effective cough continues. If the cough becomes silent or weak, or they cannot breathe or speak, give 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, leaning them forward. If back blows fail, give 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind, place a fist above the navel, grasp it with the other hand, and pull sharply inward and upward. Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the obstruction clears or the person becomes unresponsive. If they become unresponsive, lower them to the ground and begin CPR, checking the mouth for the dislodged object before each set of breaths. For an infant, use 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts. Never use abdominal thrusts on an infant. Anyone who has received abdominal thrusts should be assessed medically for internal injury.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain resuscitation council guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Hypothermia begins when core temperature falls below 35 degrees Celsius. It kills in wet, windy conditions well above freezing, so do not dismiss it in mild weather. Mild hypothermia shows as uncontrollable shivering, clumsiness, and slurred speech. The person often insists they are fine — impaired judgement is itself a symptom. Severe hypothermia shows as shivering that has stopped, rigid muscles, confusion, and a slow weak pulse. Paradoxical undressing, where the person removes clothing despite the cold, is a late and ominous sign. Move the person out of wind and rain. Remove wet clothing by cutting it off rather than making them move, and replace it with dry insulation including a hat. Insulate from the ground, which steals more heat than the air does. Put a sleeping mat, pack, or spare clothing underneath them. Give warm sweet drinks only if they are fully alert and can swallow. Never give alcohol, which dilates skin vessels and accelerates heat loss. Handle a severely hypothermic person gently and keep them horizontal. Rough handling can trigger a fatal heart rhythm. Do not rub the limbs or place them in hot water.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Environmental Emergencies
chunks.text: Heat exhaustion presents with heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, headache, nausea, cramps, and a fast weak pulse. The person is still mentally clear. Move them to shade, lie them down with legs raised, loosen clothing, and give cool water with a pinch of salt or an oral rehydration solution. Recovery should begin within 30 minutes. Heat stroke is different and is a true emergency. The key sign is altered mental state: confusion, aggression, seizures, or unconsciousness, with a core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius. The skin may be hot and dry, or still sweating. Cool aggressively and immediately. Whole-body immersion in cold water is the most effective method. Otherwise soak the person, fan them continuously, and place ice packs at the neck, armpits, and groin. Cooling in the first 30 minutes determines survival. Do not delay cooling in order to arrange transport — cool first, move second. Stop active cooling once the person becomes coherent, to avoid overshooting into hypothermia.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain wilderness medicine guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Suspect a fracture where there is deformity, grating, inability to bear weight, or pain that is sharply localised over a bone. Splint the limb in the position you found it. Do not attempt to straighten an angulated fracture unless the limb below is pale, cold, and pulseless — in which case apply gentle traction until circulation returns. A splint must immobilise the joint above and the joint below the fracture, otherwise the bone ends still move. Pad the splint well and check circulation, sensation, and movement beyond the splint before and after applying it. If fingers or toes go pale, blue, or numb, the splint is too tight. An open fracture, where bone has broken the skin, needs the wound covered with a sterile dressing and urgent antibiotics. Do not push protruding bone back inside.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Trauma and Sudden Collapse
chunks.text: Any blow to the head followed by confusion, memory loss, headache, dizziness, nausea, or visual disturbance is a concussion and needs rest and observation. Red flags requiring urgent care are: a seizure, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, unequal pupils, clear fluid from the nose or ears, weakness on one side, increasing drowsiness, or any period of unconsciousness. Deterioration can occur hours after the injury as bleeding accumulates inside the skull. Someone must stay with the person for at least 24 hours and wake them periodically. Do not give aspirin or ibuprofen after a head injury, because both interfere with clotting. Paracetamol is safer.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Burns and Poisoning
chunks.text: Cool the burn under cool running water for a full 20 minutes. This remains effective up to three hours after the injury, so start cooling even if time has passed. Twenty minutes is the target because shorter cooling does not remove enough heat from the deeper tissue, where the burn continues to extend after the flame is out. Do not use ice or iced water. Extreme cold causes further tissue damage and can drop the body temperature dangerously, especially in children. Remove clothing and jewellery from the burned area while cooling, but leave anything that is stuck to the skin in place. Cover the burn with cling film laid in flat sheets, not wrapped around a limb, or with a clean non-fluffy cloth. Wrapping tightly restricts circulation as swelling develops. Never apply butter, oil, toothpaste, or ointment to a fresh burn. These trap heat and must be painfully scrubbed off later. Do not burst blisters. Intact blisters are a sterile biological dressing. Keep the rest of the person warm while cooling the burn, because large burns lose body heat rapidly.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Burns and Poisoning
chunks.text: Suspect airway burns if there is soot around the mouth or nose, singed nasal hair, a hoarse voice, coughing black sputum, or breathing difficulty after a fire in an enclosed space. Airway swelling can develop over several hours and then close the airway rapidly. Anyone with these signs needs hospital assessment even if they feel well initially. Move to fresh air and give oxygen if available. Carbon monoxide poisoning can be present with normal-looking skin, so do not rely on colour.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain emergency care guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: Look in valley bottoms, at the base of cliffs, and where vegetation is greenest. Follow animal tracks downhill; they usually converge on water. Collect dew before dawn by dragging absorbent cloth through grass and wringing it out. A transpiration bag — a clear plastic bag tied around a leafy non-poisonous branch in sunlight — yields a small amount of clean water over a day. Rainwater collected directly in a clean container needs no treatment. Ration sweat, not water. Rest in shade during the heat of the day and travel at night; drinking your supply while working in the sun outperforms conserving it while dehydrating.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance

chunks.title: Disaster Response and Survival
chunks.text: During shaking, drop to hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table, and hold on. Do not run outside during the shaking, when falling glass and masonry cause most injuries. If you are in bed, stay there and cover your head with a pillow. If you are outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, trees, and power lines, and stay there. After the shaking stops, expect aftershocks. Check for injuries, then check for gas leaks, and shut off the gas only if you smell or hear escaping gas. Do not use matches or light switches until you are certain there is no gas leak. If you are trapped, cover your mouth, tap on a pipe or wall in a rhythmic pattern, and use a whistle if you have one. Shout only as a last resort, because it exhausts you and causes you to inhale dust.
chunks.source: Adapted from public-domain civil defence and survival guidance
